questions.q: When debugging a multithreaded program, it is generally easier to work with a version that uses as many threads as possible, so that bugs show up more often.
questions.explain: The advice is the opposite: when you can, debug a version of the program with as few threads as possible.

questions.q: You add debugging printf statements to a multithreaded program. What should each debug line include, and how should it end?
choices: The executing thread's ID, ending with \n
The process ID, ending with a tab character
The current time, with no trailing newline
The address of the shared variable, ending with a space
questions.explain: Printing the thread's ID shows which thread produced each line. Ending the line with \n keeps each thread's output on its own line.

questions.q: Each thread stores its logical ID in a local variable my_tid. What is the purpose of wrapping a debug printf in `if (my_tid == 1) { ... }`?
choices: It limits debug output to a single thread so the output is easier to read
It stops all threads except thread 1 from running
It makes the printf call thread-safe
It makes thread 1 run before the other threads
questions.explain: A condition on my_tid lets only one thread print its own information and the shared information, which cuts down the amount of debug output.

questions.q: When you debug a Pthreads program in GDB, which of these identifiers does each thread have?
choices: The Pthreads library's ID (its pthread_t value)
The operating system's lightweight process (LWP) ID
The GDB thread ID
A mutex ID assigned by pthread_mutex_t
A breakpoint number assigned by GDB
questions.explain: Each thread has at least three identifiers: its pthread_t value, its OS LWP ID, and its GDB ID. Mutexes and breakpoint numbers do not identify threads.

questions.q: Which identifier do you use to name a specific thread in a GDB command such as `thread <threadno>`?
choices: The GDB thread ID
The pthread_t value
The LWP ID
The program's own logical ID (e.g., my_tid)
questions.explain: GDB commands that name a specific thread use the GDB ID for that thread.

questions.q: What does the operating system use a thread's lightweight process (LWP) ID for?
choices: Partly to keep track of the thread for scheduling
To name the thread in GDB commands
To lock and unlock mutexes
To number the thread's breakpoints
questions.explain: The OS uses the LWP ID in part to keep track of the thread for scheduling purposes.

questions.q: The relationship between a thread's Pthreads ID, LWP ID, and GDB ID is exactly the same on every OS and Pthreads library implementation.
questions.explain: The relationship can differ between OS and Pthreads implementations. On most systems, though, there is a one-to-one-to-one correspondence between the three IDs.

questions.q: GDB prints: `[Switching to thread 3 (Thread 0x7ffff6fc3700 (LWP 5834))]`. Which statement correctly identifies the three values?
choices: 3 is the GDB ID, 0x7ffff6fc3700 is the Pthreads (pthread_t) ID, 5834 is the LWP ID
3 is the LWP ID, 0x7ffff6fc3700 is the GDB ID, 5834 is the Pthreads ID
3 is the Pthreads ID, 0x7ffff6fc3700 is the stack address, 5834 is the GDB ID
3 is the program's logical thread number, 0x7ffff6fc3700 is the LWP ID, 5834 is the process ID
questions.explain: `thread 3` uses the GDB ID. The value labeled LWP is the OS's lightweight process ID. The hex value is the pthread_t: for example, thread 0 printed pthread_id 140737345505024, which equals 0x7ffff77c4700, the value GDB showed for that thread.

questions.q: Which GDB command lists all existing threads in the program?
questions.explain: `info threads` lists every thread. The GDB thread number is the first value on each line.

questions.q: In the output of `info threads`, how is the thread that hit the breakpoint marked?
choices: With an *
With a #
With the word CURRENT
It is always listed last
questions.explain: The thread that hit the breakpoint is marked with an *.

questions.q: Which GDB command turns on printing of thread start and exit events?
questions.explain: `set print thread-events` turns on messages when threads start and exit.

questions.q: The program is stopped at a breakpoint. You want to see the stack trace of GDB thread 12. Which commands should you run?
choices: thread 12, then where
where 12
info threads 12
break where thread 12
questions.explain: `thread 12` switches to thread 12's execution context. After that, `where` prints thread 12's stack trace.

questions.q: Write the GDB command that sets a breakpoint on function foo that triggers only when GDB thread 12 runs it.
questions.explain: The syntax is `break <where> thread <threadno>`.

questions.q: You set `break 77 thread 4`. What happens when thread 2 executes line 77?
choices: Nothing: the breakpoint does not trigger, and thread 2 keeps running
The program pauses and GDB switches to thread 4
The program pauses at the breakpoint in thread 2
GDB prints a warning and deletes the breakpoint
questions.explain: A thread-specific breakpoint fires only for the named thread. Other threads that reach that point in the code do not pause the program.

questions.q: What does adding the prefix `thread apply <threadno|all>` to a GDB command do?
choices: It runs the command on the given thread(s), or on all threads
It creates a new thread to run the command
It switches permanently to the given thread
It makes the command run only after all threads exit
questions.explain: `thread apply <threadno|all> command` runs a GDB command on one thread, a subset of threads, or all threads, using GDB thread IDs.

questions.q: The correct way to set a breakpoint on foo for only thread 3 is `thread apply 3 break foo`.
questions.explain: `thread apply` does not work for every GDB command, and setting breakpoints is one of the exceptions. Use `break foo thread 3` instead.

questions.q: By default, what does GDB do when one thread reaches a breakpoint?
choices: It pauses all threads until the user types cont
It pauses only the thread that hit the breakpoint
It pauses only the main thread
It kills every thread except the one that hit the breakpoint
questions.explain: By default, GDB pauses all threads until the user continues. You can change this so that only the threads that hit a breakpoint pause.

questions.q: You can configure GDB so that only the threads that hit a breakpoint pause and the other threads keep running.
questions.explain: The user can change the default behavior so that only threads that hit a breakpoint pause, and the other threads keep running.

questions.q: Several threads in racecond.c run `count += i;` on a shared variable count. Two runs with 5 threads print different final values for count. What is the cause?
choices: A race condition: there is no synchronization around accesses to the shared variable count
Each thread has its own private copy of count
The loop bound differs from one run to the next
printf changes the value of count
questions.explain: Nothing synchronizes access to count, so concurrent updates interfere with each other. That race condition makes the final result differ from run to run.

questions.q: What is the fix for the race condition on count in racecond.c?
choices: Put accesses to count inside a critical section protected by a pthread_mutex_t
Declare count as a local variable in main
Have each thread call printf after updating count
Use thread-specific breakpoints on the line that updates count
questions.explain: Wrapping the accesses to count in a critical section with a pthread_mutex_t lets only one thread update it at a time.

questions.q: In GDB, the racecond program is started with `run 3`, so it spawns three threads. What is the GDB thread number of the main thread?
questions.explain: The main thread is always GDB thread 1. The three spawned threads are GDB threads 2 to 4.

questions.q: With `break main`, GDB stops at the start of main. Why can't you set `break 77 thread 4` at that point?
choices: Only thread 1 (the main thread) exists yet, so thread 4 has not been created
Thread-specific breakpoints can only be set on function names
Line 77 has not been compiled yet
You must delete breakpoint 1 first
questions.explain: You have to keep track of which threads exist. At the breakpoint in main, only thread 1 exists, so you must wait until the other threads are created before setting a breakpoint for one of them.

questions.q: In the session, thread 4 stops at `count += i;` and `print i` shows 1. Then you run `thread 3` and `print i`, which shows 0. Why is the value different?
choices: i is a local variable, so each thread has its own copy on its own stack, and print shows the current thread's i
The thread command resets every local variable to 0
Thread 3 has not started running yet
print i always shows the main thread's value
questions.explain: Each thread has its own stack and its own local i. After `thread 3`, commands like `print` and `where` work in thread 3's context.

questions.q: The program printed `hello I'm thread 0 with pthread_id 140737345505024`, and GDB earlier showed `[New Thread 0x7ffff77c4700 (LWP 5833)]`. In this session, 0x7ffff77c4700 == 140737345505024, and LWP 5833 matches GDB thread 2. Which GDB thread is the program's logical thread 0?
choices: GDB thread 2
GDB thread 1
GDB thread 0
GDB thread 4
questions.explain: The program's own numbering (myid) is separate from GDB's. Logical thread 0 has the same pthread_t and LWP ID (5833) as GDB thread 2. GDB thread 1 is always the main thread.

questions.q: After `break 77 thread 4` and `cont`, thread 4 stops at line 77 (`count += i;`) and `print i` shows 0. After another `cont`, thread 4 stops at line 77 again and `print i` shows 1. Why does it stop at the same line again?
choices: Line 77 is the body of a for loop, so the breakpoint fires each time thread 4 runs it on a new iteration
cont restarts the thread from the beginning of worker_loop
A thread-specific breakpoint fires exactly twice and is then deleted
Another thread hit the breakpoint and GDB reported it as thread 4
questions.explain: Line 77 is inside `for (i = 0; i < 10000; i++)`. Each time thread 4 runs it, the breakpoint fires, so you see i = 0 and then i = 1. Other threads do not trigger the breakpoint.
